observations: Code coverage frameworks (Datadog, coverage.py, PHPUnit) support multiple coverage definitions (line, branch, path, condition) with configurable aggregation recipes (set union, weighted merge, per-module thresholds). The choice of which coverage metric and how to aggregate across test suites is a well-documented recipe choice ambiguity.

Information retrieval has the most direct parallel: micro-averaging vs macro-averaging vs weighted averaging of precision/recall/F1 across classes is a textbook recipe choice problem. The Stanford NLP textbook (Manning et al.) explicitly documents that 'the differences between the two methods can be large' and that 'microaveraged results are really a measure of effectiveness on the large classes.' Two distinct 'macro F1' formulas exist (averaged-F1 vs F1-of-averages) diverging by up to 0.5 in extreme cases (ar5iv:1911.03347).

Web analytics has recipe choice ambiguity in engagement metrics: GA4 redefined bounce rate from 'single-page sessions' (UA) to 'non-engaged sessions' (GA4), changing the recipe entirely. Session duration vs engagement time vs time-on-page are different recipes measuring different things. The choice of which metric to report changes the conclusion.

SPIDER's density metric recipe choice maps directly to the micro/macro/weighted aggregation distinction in IR. Per-iteration canonical recipe (uniform p=0.5 across definitions) is analogous to micro-averaging (equal weight per observation/iteration). Per-task weighted recipe is analogous to macro-averaging (equal weight per task/group). Both answer legitimate scientific questions: micro asks 'do definitions disagree more than random across all iterations?' while macro asks 'do definitions disagree more than random within each task on average?'

The principled resolution across all three fields is consistent: recipe choice is a design decision, not an implementation detail. Each recipe answers a different scientific question. The resolution is to (1) state which recipe you use, (2) justify it by the question you are answering, (3) report sensitivity to recipe choice when possible. This directly informs SPIDER's density metric approach.
validity_notes: This is a literature synthesis experiment with no new empirical measurement. Claim ceiling is bounded to published literature only.

Literature search used web search (Google Scholar, ACM DL, arXiv references) with keyword-based queries. Not a systematic review with formal inclusion/exclusion criteria, but sufficient for the bounded claim ceiling.

Code coverage evidence comes from framework documentation (Datadog, coverage.py, PHPUnit, BullseyeCoverage) rather than peer-reviewed papers, but the recipe choice ambiguity is well-documented in these primary sources.
IR evidence is strongest: Stanford NLP textbook (Manning et al.), scikit-learn documentation, and ar5iv:1911.03347 (Sokolova & Lapalme) provide rigorous analysis of aggregation recipe ambiguity.
Web analytics evidence comes from Google Analytics documentation, industry analyses, and comparative studies (PMC9140287). The GA4 vs UA bounce rate definitional change is well-documented.

The applicability mapping (SPIDER density metric → IR micro/macro/weighted) is an interpretation by the producer, not an established result. The mapping is principled but requires validation by downstream audit.
unresolved: Whether the micro/macro/weighted framework from IR is the OPTIMAL resolution framework for SPIDER's density metric recipe choice, or whether a different framework (e.g., information-theoretic, Bayesian) would be more appropriate
Whether reporting sensitivity to recipe choice (both recipes as co-primary) is sufficient, or whether a third recipe (meta-analytic combination) is needed
